metadata.notes: agent=yes, daemon=full, driver=gap:keys — a plainly non-mutating bash call (a shell for-loop wrapping only `ls`/`cat`) live-confirmed to leave the policy fast-track and open a genuine, separately-resolved approval gate, distinguishable in the same session from a mutating call's own gate. The discriminator is shell syntactic shape (control-flow constructs escalate to review) and specific dangerous verbs (rm), NOT read-vs-write or workspace containment — both of those hypotheses were tested live and falsified.

assessment.body:
## Verdict

agent_supports: yes; daemon_capability: full; driver_capability: gap:keys

## The question this cell asks, answered empirically

The cell asks whether a plainly non-mutating tool call (a read, a search, a listing) ever leaves muse's policy fast-track and produces its own genuine `waiting` episode, or whether reads are structurally exempt from ever gating (which would make this scenario unrecordable for muse). I did not reason from the `:auto-review` profile name; I drove muse live in three throwaway directories outside the repo (via tmux, `--trust-workspace --approval-judge off`, matching the load-bearing precondition 2-19/tool-gate-permission-prompt already established) and tested competing hypotheses against real `side_effect_intent.policy_decision` and `kind:"approval"` records.

**Hypothesis 1 (read vs write) — FALSIFIED.** A bare, single, non-compound `touch ./mutate-marker.txt` (a MUTATING call — it creates a file) got `policy_decision:"allow:policy"` with zero approval record, identical to a bare `cat <file>` and a bare `git log --oneline` (both pure reads). All three single-verb invocations fast-tracked regardless of their read/write nature. A `&&`-chain of four read-only commands (`cat readme.txt && ls -la && git log --oneline && git diff --stat`) ALSO fast-tracked. So "is this call a read" is not muse's discriminator at all.

**Hypothesis 2 (workspace containment) — FALSIFIED.** `cat` of a file OUTSIDE the session's workspace root (a throwaway file in the scratchpad, well outside the launched cwd) also got `allow:policy` with no approval — the scenario description's own suggested example ("a file read outside the workspace") does not gate muse's `bash`/`cat` path; `canonical_workspace_root` containment is not what forces review here.

**Hypothesis 3 (shell control-flow syntax) — CONFIRMED, reproducibly.** A `for` loop whose body is a PURE READ (`for f in readme.txt; do cat $f; done`, and independently `for d in .; do ls -la "$d"; done` — a plain directory listing, the scenario's own other suggested example, with no file dependency at all) reliably produced a real `kind:"approval"` `"requested"` record with the TUI dialog "Would you like to run the following command? … 1. Yes, proceed 2. No", resolved by a raw `"1"` keypress (no Enter — confirmed applies on keydown, same as 2-19) into `decision_applied` with `decision_source.kind:"human_approval"`. This is NOT a novel construction I invented: the pre-existing corpus already contains two examples of exactly this shape — session `01a09c71-ab1c-...` (this machine, recorded before this assessment pass, under the DEFAULT `:auto-review` profile with the judge ON, not the `--approval-judge off` override) has TWO `kind:"approval"` `"requested"` records whose `raw_command` is a `for … ; do … ; done` loop wrapping only `cat`/`grep`/`echo`/`source` — zero mutating verbs in either. So the read-escapes-fast-track behavior is a genuine, pre-existing muse policy characteristic, not an artifact of my probe's flags.

**Both gates, same session, cleanly distinguishable, sequential (not batched).** I drove a single turn asking muse to run the read-only for-loop FIRST, then the mutating `touch ./gate-marker.txt && rm -rf ./gate-marker.txt && echo done` (the exact command 2-19 already validated as a real mutating gate) as a SEPARATE, later tool call. Session `01a09f33-4bd2-7e51-8f1a-561e85ae7fe4` (this machine, this assessment pass) shows the model naturally serializing the two tool calls (no `--parallel-tool-calls`): sequence 61 opens the read-only gate, sequence 63 closes it (`human_approval`), the tool result is delivered back to the model (sequence 76), the model THEN proposes the second tool call (sequence 104), sequence 107 opens the mutating gate — presented with a DIFFERENT, richer dialog ("Stage 2/3, Current argv: [\"rm\",\"-rf\",…], 1. Allow this stage once / 2. Always allow in this workspace / 3. Abort") confirming the two gates are not just two instances of the same dialog — sequence 110 closes it (`human_approval` again), and the turn completes to a final reply and terminal (`turn_duration_ms:67533`). This is exactly the scenario's canonical single-turn arc: ready → working → waiting → working → waiting → working → ready, with NO batching risk (muse never pre-raised the second dialog before the first was answered).

## Why: the working model of muse's classifier (not fully reverse-engineered, stated as a caveat)

A single, non-compound bash invocation of a recognized low-risk verb (`ls`, `cat`, `git log`, `touch`, and apparently arbitrary `&&`-chains of such verbs) resolves via a static policy layer to `allow:policy` regardless of read/write semantics. Two independent things escalate to a real approval regardless of that: (a) a shell CONTROL-FLOW construct the static classifier can't fully resolve (a `for` loop, confirmed twice live plus twice in the pre-existing corpus — untested whether `while`/`if`/`case` behave the same, and NOT claimed here) forces review even when everything inside is a read; (b) a recognized dangerous verb (`rm`, evaluated PER-STAGE even inside an `&&`-chain whose other stages — `touch`, `echo` — are individually safe: "Skipped Stage 1/3: matched mode:on_request … Stage 2/3 … Current argv: [\"rm\",\"-rf\",…]") forces review for that one stage. A `session-evidence.py` doctor-skill script bundled inside the muse binary (`strings` extraction, not confirmed to be the SAME code path as the live Rust policy engine) independently names `DIRECT_MUTATORS = {apply_patch, delete_file, edit_file, write_file}` and `SHELL_MUTATORS = {cp, git, install, mv, rm, rmdir, sed, tee, truncate, unlink}` — consistent with, but not proof of, mechanism (b); it is cited as corroborating vocabulary, not as the live classifier's source.

## Daemon

`core/adapters/inbound/agents/muse/parser.go`'s `parseApprovalRequested`/`parseApprovalDecisionApplied` (already cited by 2-19) key ONLY on `pending_action_id` — no branch on `tool_name`, `raw_command`, or `decision_source`. The live single-session recording above shows BOTH the read-only-for-loop gate and the mutating-rm gate producing byte-shape-identical `kind:"approval"` `requested`→`decision_applied` pairs; the daemon's `TranscriptPermissionPending`/`transcript_permission_prompt` rule (state_classifier.go, same mechanism 2-19 and copilot's #1256 already exercise) cannot distinguish and does not need to — both episodes map to `waiting` the same way. `daemon_capability=full`, no daemon work needed, no known bug.

## Driver

Same two gaps 2-19 already named and which this cell reuses rather than re-deriving: `keys` is stubbed `not_implemented` in `replaydata/agents/muse/driver-interactive.sh` (line ~671, absent from `DRIVE_ELICITS` at line 167), and `--approval-judge` has no settings-driven launch-arg wiring yet (only `.model`/`.base_url` are wired, lines ~91-125). Both are small, mechanical additions `record` ports before this cell can run — identical shape to 2-19's, not a fresh gap.

## Vacuous-pass check

Under what condition would this cell pass while proving nothing? If the recipe's "read-only" call were instead something that ALSO happens to be a recognized SHELL_MUTATOR-adjacent construct, the recording would show two waiting episodes but would not actually demonstrate a genuinely non-mutating call escaping the fast track — it would just be a second mutating-flavored gate wearing a read-only label. The recipe's read-only call (`for d in .; do ls -la "$d"; done`) is deliberately zero-mutation at every level: `ls` is not in any observed mutator list, the loop touches nothing on disk, and it was independently reproduced with a second, differently-shaped command (`for f in readme.txt; do cat $f; done`) and cross-checked against two pre-existing corpus examples recorded before this assessment pass began — four independent occurrences of "for-loop wrapping pure reads escalates to review" is not a coincidence of one crafted prompt.
caveats: LOAD-BEARING PRECONDITION (shared with 2-19): the recipe's settings.approval_judge:"off" makes the gates resolve via a genuine human decision the driver can deterministically time `keys` against. It is NOT required for the underlying daemon finding — the pre-existing corpus shows the SAME for-loop-escapes-fast-track behavior under the DEFAULT judge-ON profile too (session 01a09c71-ab1c-..., decision_source.kind:"llm_judge") — but under judge-ON the dialog can resolve automatically in ~8-30s before a fixed-delay driver script's `keys` step fires, which would misdirect the keypress. Re-probe decision_source.kind at record time exactly as 2-19 already flags.

The EXACT ruleset that escalates a shell command to review is not fully reverse-engineered. Only `for` loops were tested (4 independent occurrences: 2 live, 2 pre-existing corpus); `while`/`if`/`case`/command substitution were not tried and may or may not behave the same. The recipe's specific `for d in .; do ls -la "$d"; done` is the load-bearing, reproducible artifact — do not substitute an untested construct at record time without re-verifying it still gates.

driver=gap:keys AND no settings-driven --approval-judge launch-arg wiring yet — both are real, small, mechanical driver additions record must port, identical to 2-19's already-documented gap (not a new one; do not double-count).

The read-only gate's TUI dialog ("Would you like to run the following command? 1. Yes 2. No") is SIMPLER than the mutating gate's ("Stage N/3, Current argv: […], 1. Allow this stage once / 2. Always allow / 3. Abort") — both resolve to "1" but the driver's `keys` step must not assume they're the same widget shape if a future driver tries to parse the screen rather than blind-key.

muse spawns companion reminder-agent child sessions freely during any turn (muse-assess-context.md; also observed live here — memory_reminder_child_session_linked records on both turns). Every phase in the spec is pinned same_session_as:session_birth to rule out the vacuous-pass mechanism 2-2/2-17/2-19 all had to guard against.
cost_nonzero must stay false: muse-spark-1.3-contributor has no pricing/alias entry (core/pkg/capacity), the established muse-wide fact copied here rather than re-derived per-cell.

Not independently re-verified whether a native (non-bash) read call — `read_file` on a path outside the workspace — gates the same way; the recipe uses bash's `ls`/`cat` because that path is the one confirmed live and reachable without porting additional driver primitives. `read_file`'s own containment behavior (binary strings suggest it may simply REFUSE out-of-workspace paths rather than gate them) is UNVERIFIED and out of scope for this recipe.

script.text:
Do exactly these two steps using the bash tool, one at a time, as two SEPARATE tool calls. Wait for step 1's tool result before starting step 2; do not batch them together and do not use any tool other than bash.
Step 1: run exactly this command as one tool call: for d in .; do ls -la "$d"; done
Step 2: run exactly this command as a separate, later tool call: touch ./gate-marker.txt && rm -rf ./gate-marker.txt && echo done
Do not run anything else and do not re-verify afterward. When both steps are done, reply with exactly this single line and nothing else: PERMISSION_GATE_NONMUTATING_OK

verify: events.jsonl shows the full ready->working->waiting->working->waiting->working->ready arc on the SAME session_id born at start

the FIRST state_transition to waiting corresponds to the read-only for-loop's approval (session.jsonl decision_applied for that pending_action_id has decision_source.kind=="human_approval", re-probed at record time)
the SECOND state_transition to waiting corresponds to the mutating touch&&rm's approval (same decision_source check)
the two waiting episodes are separated by a state_transition to working (the tool result delivery + second tool-call proposal between them) — they must not merge into one episode
events.jsonl contains no state_transition to waiting after the final ready is reached
transcript shows the literal final reply token 'PERMISSION_GATE_NONMUTATING_OK'
